objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how a learner moves from instrument to visual flight at the DA or MDA and keeps it to a stop, teach the division of attention that makes that switch safe, brief the environmental, operational and weather factors and the ATC advisories (NOTAMs, wind shear, wake turbulence, runway surface and braking) that change the landing, coach the checklist and the turn to final, demonstrate the landing while explaining it, and spot and fix a learner's transition, checklist, turn-to-final, wind and control errors.
why: Approach lights are the basic means of changing from instrument to visual flight for landing [[33:121|AIM 2-1-1]]; the IFH calls the decision to land or go missed the most critical period of the approach [[23:281|IFH 9-38]], and the IPH says single-pilot operations make the transition even more challenging [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. Below the DA or MDA there is no implicit obstacle protection, so the pilot must see and avoid [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]]. The PTS also tells the evaluator to emphasize your ability to teach wake turbulence and low-level wind shear avoidance, checklist usage and positive exchange of flight controls (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction), and all of them meet in this Task.

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner flies a perfect ILS to minimums, you lift the view-limiting device, and within a few seconds the airplane is 10 knots slow, drifting left of the centerline and sinking below the glidepath while the learner stares at the runway lights. What went wrong in those seconds, and how would you have briefed and coached the switch to outside references?

chunks.title: The visual segment: what this Task adds

body.p: The Instrument lesson IR.VI.E covers the pilot's side of this landing; this lesson adds how you teach it. The evaluator selects Tasks A and B and combines them with Task C, D or E, and may ask for a landing or a missed approach at the end of each approach (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area VIII NOTE and Introduction). Task E is the ending where the approach continues to a landing on the runway it serves.

**Two stages.** The IFH divides an ILS approach into an instrument stage flown on radio guidance and a visual stage, where visual contact with the runway environment is needed for accuracy and safety. The most critical period is the point where the pilot decides to land or go missed [[23:281|IFH 9-38]]. The visual segment begins at the DA or MDA and continues to the runway, flown by natural vision under 14 CFR 91.175(c) or with an enhanced flight vision system under 91.176 [[29:160|IPH 4-20]]. This lesson teaches natural vision.

callout.text: Approaches with vertical guidance make the transition safer because the airplane is already stabilized when the references appear [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. On a nonprecision approach the learner must plan where to leave the MDA, and a descent below it between the VDP and the MAP may be inadvisable or impossible [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h3]]. Lesson FII.VIII.A covers that planning.

check.q: Your learner says the approach is over once the runway is in sight. How do you correct that from the sources?
check.a: The visual segment from the DA or MDA to the runway is part of the approach [[29:160|IPH 4-20]], the decision to land or go missed is its most critical point [[23:281|IFH 9-38]], and below minimums the pilot must see and avoid obstacles because there is no implicit obstacle protection [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]].

body.p: **Transition to, and maintenance of, a visual flight condition** starts with a legal test. Below the authorized MDA, or continuing below the DA/DH, the pilot needs all three of these [[60:471|14 CFR 91.175(c)]]:

bullets: The aircraft is continuously in a position to descend to a landing on the intended runway at a normal rate of descent using normal maneuvers [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].
The flight visibility is not less than the visibility in the approach being used [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2)]].

At least one listed visual reference for the intended runway is distinctly visible and identifiable [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]]. With only the approach lights, not below 100 ft above TDZE unless the red terminating bars or red side row bars are also visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]].

callout.text: Landing: no pilot may land when the flight visibility is less than the visibility in the approach procedure being used [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(d)(2)]]. Missed approach: immediately, whenever the paragraph (c) requirements are not met below the MDA, or on arrival at the missed approach point (including a DA) and any time after that until touchdown [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]].

body.p: **Maintenance is the word learners miss.** The test is "continuously" in position, and the missed approach rule runs "until touchdown" [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]. Once below the DA, DH or MDA, a missed approach is required if the visibility is lost or the runway environment goes out of sight; a rejected landing for people, equipment or animals on the runway, or because the approach became unstabilized, also means flying a missed approach [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]. Only the pilot can judge flight visibility, and if it is below the chart value the pilot goes missed whatever the reported visibility [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. For Part 121 and 135 operations the descent rate must also allow touchdown in the touchdown zone [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]].

**Straight-in or circling minimums.** Straight-in minimums are published only when the final course is within 30° of the runway and a normal descent is possible. A straight-in landing may still be made from a circling-only approach when the runway is in sight in time for a normal approach and ATC has cleared the landing [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]].

callout.text: Application: make the three tests a spoken decision at minimums, such as "Approach lights, visibility good, in position: continuing," or "Missed approach." A spoken decision is easy to grade, and a missing one shows you where the learner's attention was.

check.q: At the DA your learner sees only a MALSR, which has no red bars, and continues. Where must something more be in sight?
check.a: At 100 ft above TDZE. Below that the approach lights alone are not enough without red terminating or side row bars [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]], and a MALSR has none [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]], so another listed reference, such as the threshold or runway lights, must be in sight [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]].

chunks.title: Transition to, and maintenance of, a visual flight condition

body.p: **The hard part.** The IPH calls the transition from instrument to visual flight very challenging, especially in low visibility, and warns that shallow fog may leave too little visibility to flare [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. In a two-pilot crew the pilot flying stays on the instruments while most of the pilot monitoring's attention goes outside from 100 to 200 ft above minimums; the pilot monitoring calls the visual aids or "runway in sight," and then calls the vertical speed while the pilot flying goes visual [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. A single pilot must keep flying by instruments while trying to acquire the references, so dividing attention is even more critical [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].
Application: turn the crew model into a single-pilot sequence the learner can say and fly.

body.p: **Reading the picture.** On a stabilized approach the runway keeps the same shape as it grows; if it seems to shorten and widen the approach is getting shallow, and if it lengthens and narrows it is getting steep [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. The aiming point does not move in the windshield, and its distance from the horizon stays constant [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

**Why the transition goes wrong.** Optical illusions are primarily associated with landing, exactly when the pilot changes from instruments to outside cues [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. Rain on the windscreen and featureless terrain make the pilot feel high and fly low; haze makes the runway seem farther away and also leads low; flying into fog feels like a pitch-up and leads to an abruptly steeper approach [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. In the AWH's analysis of a wind shear accident, the switch from instruments to outside references may have detracted from the instrument scan [[28:272|AWH 22-17]].

callout.text: Application: give the learner one rule to say aloud: "The instruments fly until a required reference is identified; then outside flies and the instruments check." It keeps the scan running through the switch instead of a one-look change [[29:179|IPH 4-39]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

check.q: Night, light rain, dark terrain around the airport. Which way will the illusions push your learner after the transition, and what keeps them honest?
check.a: Low: rain on the windscreen and featureless terrain both create an illusion of being higher than you are [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. Use the VASI, PAPI or electronic glideslope, check the altimeter often and use the VDP [[23:76|IFH 3-9]] [[23:77|IFH 3-10]].

body.p: Flight instructors must guide learners in how to divide their attention, and the IFH says the importance of this division of attention, or cross-check, cannot be overemphasized [[23:342|IFH B-1]]. Application: no source gives a single-pilot method for the visual transition, so build it in the steps below.

body.p: **The view-limiting device.** The PTS has the applicant and evaluator brief when and how the device goes on and comes off, and says the device does not apply to elements of a Task that need visual references (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Application: brief the same thing with every learner, for example, "At minimums I'll say 'look up' if the references would be in sight; until then, stay on the gauges," and agree what you will say if they would not be. The safety pilot must have adequate vision forward and to each side, or a competent observer must supplement it [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

**Keep the instruments in the landing.** The AIH notes that habitual attention to instrument indications leads to better landings through more precise airspeed control [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. A learner who never checks airspeed after looking up shows the cross-check faults the IFH names: fixation, staring at a single instrument (here, the runway), and omission, dropping an instrument from the scan [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

callout.text: Application: a sudden lift of the device at minimums teaches a one-look switch. Also practice glance-and-return transitions so the scan keeps running, and guard the controls closely in the last few hundred feet: the learner must never exceed your limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Your learner's approaches are perfect until you lift the device; then the airspeed wanders 10 knots. Name the problem and the fix for the next lesson.
check.a: A division of attention error: the scan stopped at the transition, likely fixation on the runway or omission of the airspeed indicator [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Teach the single-pilot rule of flying by instruments while acquiring the references [[29:179|IPH 4-39]], then a spoken airspeed check after looking up and periodic airspeed glances on final [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: **Effect of specific environmental, operational, and meteorological factors.** Teach them as three questions the learner answers before the approach: what is outside, what are the airplane and the runway doing, and what is the weather doing. Before any flight the pilot in command must know runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

body.p: Adverse winds cause many weather-related accidents, and takeoff and landing are the phases most exposed to them [[28:116|AWH 10-1]]. The most critical landing conditions combine high gross weight, high density altitude and unfavorable wind [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

callout.text: Application: turn the table into a pre-approach question set the learner answers aloud every time: "What will the runway look like? What will push me low? How does today's landing distance compare with the runway? What is the surface wind doing?" It builds the hazard-identification habit the PTS wants the evaluator to see (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

check.q: Your learner plans a night ILS to a 75 ft wide runway after training on 150 ft runways. What illusion do you brief, and what is the defense?
check.a: A narrower runway creates an illusion of being higher, so the pilot flies a lower approach and risks striking objects or landing short [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. Stay on the glideslope or VGSI and check the altimeter often [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

chunks.title: ATC advisories: NOTAMs, ATIS, runway surface and braking

body.p: **Adherence to ATC advisories, such as NOTAMs, wind shear, wake turbulence, runway surface, and braking conditions.** The first advisory is read before departure: 14 CFR 91.103 requires familiarity with all available information, including NOTAMs, which can affect runways, taxiways, obstructions, communications, NAVAIDs and anything else essential to landing operations [[33:324|AIM 5-1-3]]. ATIS gives the wind, visibility, weather, altimeter setting, and the approach and runway in use, and it is updated with each official hourly and special weather report and re-recorded for changes such as the runway or approach in use [[33:212|AIM 4-1-13]] [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13]].

body.p: **Wet runways.** Water reduces braking and can remove it when the tires hydroplane [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. The minimum dynamic hydroplaning speed is about 9 times the square root of the main tire pressure, so 36 psi gives 54 knots, and once started, hydroplaning can continue well below that speed [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. Teach a grooved runway if available, a touchdown as slow as is safe, moderate braking after the nosewheel is down, and aerodynamic drag if the airplane is not slowing [[24:209|AFH 9-38]].

callout.text: Application: have the learner read each runway advisory back in plain words and say what it changes: "Medium on the roll-out third, so I touch down at my point at the right speed, and if I'm long I go around." The AIM puts the suitability judgment on the pilot, not on the report [[33:251|AIM 4-3-9]].

check.q: ATIS says braking action advisories are in effect, but the tower gives your learner no report. What should the learner do?
check.a: Ask for current runway condition information; pilots should be prepared for deteriorating braking and request the information if controllers do not issue it [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8]].

chunks.title: Wind shear: the advisory and the technique

body.p: **Wind shear** is a change in wind speed or direction over a short distance, of greatest concern on takeoff and landing, and typically found with thunderstorms and low-level temperature inversions, with jet streams and fronts as other sources [[23:316|IFH 10-25]]. On an instrument approach a tailwind shearing to a headwind raises airspeed, pitches the nose up and balloons the airplane above the glidepath; a headwind shearing to a tailwind does the opposite, and the airplane sinks below it [[23:316|IFH 10-25]].

**The deadly sequence.** A headwind shear followed by a tailwind or downdraft is particularly dangerous: the pilot who reduced power and lowered the nose for the headwind is left nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits [[23:316|IFH 10-25]]. Microburst downdrafts can reach 6,000 fpm, with up to a 90 knot headwind-to-tailwind shear across the microburst, and a microburst intensifies for about 5 minutes after it strikes the ground [[34:108|AIM 7-1-24]].

Figure 22-21 shows why wind shear belongs in this Task: the encounter comes at the transition from instruments to visual, where reduced visual cues and the airspeed loss combine into a pitch reduction [[28:271|AWH 22-16]]. Pitch increase and recovery started too late; the transition may have detracted from the instrument scan, and the AWH says a stabilized approach with clearly defined callouts is essential to recognize unacceptable flightpath trends [[28:272|AWH 22-17]].

bullets: **ATC alerts.** LLWAS gives the airport wind followed by the boundary wind; newer systems give alerts such as "Runway 17 arrival microburst alert, 40 knot loss 3 mile final" [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7]] [[33:250|AIM 4-3-7]].

**Limits.** Basic LLWAS detects wind shear only around the airport's periphery and gives no microburst alerts; the Chart Supplement lists airports with LLWAS, ITWS or WSP [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7]] [[33:250|AIM 4-3-7]].

**Cockpit cues.** A rapid or large airspeed increase near convective weather may announce a coming loss and may be reason to discontinue the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]; a stabilized approach helps the pilot recognize abnormal indications [[29:177|IPH 4-37]].
**Visual signs.** Heavy rain, light rain in virga, or only a ring of blowing dust [[34:108|AIM 7-1-24]].
**Reporting.** State the airspeed loss or gain and the altitude; avoid "negative" or "positive" wind shear [[34:106|AIM 7-1-22]].

callout.text: **Improper technique for wind shear.** The sources' answer is to be alert early in the approach and ready to go missed at the first indication: recovery at low altitude may be impossible, and some microbursts cannot be escaped with any known technique [[23:316|IFH 10-25]] [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. Do not land in the face of an approaching thunderstorm [[28:276|AWH 22-21]].

check.q: Near a rain shaft on a 3-mile final, airspeed jumps 15 knots and the airplane balloons above the glideslope. Your learner pulls the power back. What do you teach?
check.a: A large airspeed increase near convective weather may be the first sign of a coming loss and may be reason to discontinue the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. Reducing power and lowering the nose for the headwind sets up the nose-low, power-low state when the tailwind hits, so be ready to go missed at the first indication [[23:316|IFH 10-25]].

chunks.title: Wake turbulence behind the airplane ahead

body.p: **Wake turbulence.** Every aircraft producing lift trails two counter-rotating vortices, and the induced roll can exceed the roll control of the aircraft that meets them [[34:147|AIM 7-4-1]]. The strongest vortices come from a heavy, clean, slow aircraft, and airplanes with a short wingspan relative to the generating aircraft find the roll harder to counter [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]] [[34:148|AIM 7-4-3]].

Vortices begin at rotation and end at touchdown, sink several hundred feet per minute, and close to the ground move sideways at 2 or 3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]. A cross-runway wind of 1 to 5 knots can hold the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone, and a tailwind can move vortices forward into it; the light quartering tailwind requires maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

body.p: **The ATC advisory.** Tower controllers give VFR aircraft that may be affected the larger aircraft's position, altitude and direction followed by "CAUTION - WAKE TURBULENCE," but whether or not a warning is given, the pilot is expected to adjust the flight path to prevent serious wake encounters [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Accepting traffic information, an instruction to follow an aircraft, or a visual approach clearance means accepting responsibility for wake turbulence separation [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]].

callout.text: Application: on a straight-in behind a jet, ask before the FAF: "Where will its wake be, and where will you touch down?" The AIM asks pilots of aircraft with strong wakes to fly on the glidepath, not above it [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]], so the learner who stays at or above that path and lands beyond the jet's touchdown point is following the AIM [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

check.q: Your learner is cleared to land 4 miles behind a Boeing 737 on the same runway with a light quartering tailwind. What two things do you want in the plan?
check.a: Stay at or above the 737's final approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]], with maximum caution because a light quartering tailwind can move its vortices forward into the touchdown zone [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

chunks.title: Crosswind and gusts after the break-out

body.p: **Crosswind.** The AFH gives two methods: the crab, removed with rudder just before touchdown, and the wing-low (sideslip) method, recommended in most cases. On a long final the pilot can crab first and change smoothly to wing-low before the round out [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

With wing-low, rudder aligns the nose with the runway and aileron stops the drift; the upwind wing stays down through the round out, and the touchdown is on the upwind main wheel [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. If full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn, the wind is too strong for that runway and the landing must be made on a better runway or at an alternate [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. Airplanes are tested to be controllable in 90° crosswinds up to 0.2 VSO, and the demonstrated value is placarded on airplanes certificated after May 3, 1962 [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

**Gusts and turbulence.** Use a power-on approach slightly above normal approach speed and partial flaps in a gusty crosswind. Pilots often add one-half the gust factor: "If the normal speed is 70 knots, and the wind gusts are 15 knots, an increase of airspeed to 77 knots is appropriate," always within the AFM/POH [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Keep power on until the main wheels touch, because closing the throttle early in turbulence can cause a sudden sink and a hard landing [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. A gust raises airspeed and lift and may balloon the airplane, and the lull that follows makes it sink [[28:132|AWH 10-17]].

callout.text: Application: brief that, crabbed on final, the runway will appear on the downwind side of the nose when the lights come into view. A learner who turns the nose toward it removes the wind correction and drifts downwind of the centerline. Keep the track on the centerline, then change to wing-low.

check.q: Crabbed 10° on an ILS, your learner breaks out and immediately rolls wings level with the nose on the runway, no sideslip. What happens, and what do you teach?
check.a: The airplane drifts downwind; inadequate compensation for wind drift on final and touching down while drifting are listed crosswind errors [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Keep the track on the centerline, then use rudder to align the nose and aileron to stop the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

chunks.title: The turn to final: plan it, then fly it

body.p: **Failure to properly plan and perform the turn to final approach.** On a straight-in instrument approach the turn to final is usually the intercept of the final approach course. The approach clearance normally comes with the final vector, chosen so the airplane is established on the final course before the FAF [[33:396|AIM 5-4-3b1(c)]]. Controllers vector to intercept at least 2 NM outside the approach gate, a point one mile outside the FAF; closer intercepts are allowed when the ceiling is at least 500 ft above the MVA/MIA and the visibility at least 3 SM (no closer than the gate), or when the pilot asks (no closer than the FAF), but those exceptions do not apply to RNAV aircraft vectored for a GPS or RNAV approach [[29:193|IPH 4-53]] [[29:194|IPH 4-54]].

bullets: **Plan it.** Know the final course, the intercept heading and the cue to start the turn. With practice judging the rate of closure, pilots learn to lead the turn to prevent overshooting the course [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

**Localizer.** The course is normally 5° wide, full scale at 2.5° either side, so the needle is very sensitive and corrections must shrink as the course narrows [[23:280|IFH 9-37]] [[23:283|IFH 9-40]].

**GPS.** Over- or under-banking the turn onto final can delay getting on course and cause high descent rates later; vectors that intercept within 2 NM of the FAWP are not recommended [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(4)]] [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]].

**Offset final.** An LDA is not aligned with the runway and needs more maneuvering than an ILS; straight-in minimums are published only up to a 30° offset [[33:80|AIM 1-1-9c]] [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]]. Below the MDA the amount of turn is one of the factors in whether a safe descent and landing is possible [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5h3]].

body.p: **The visual turn.** When the last turn is flown visually, the AFH errors apply: an overshooting, undershooting, too steep or too shallow turn onto final, and a skidding turn from base to final [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. A skidding cross-control stall is most likely in a poorly planned base-to-final turn, often after an unrecognized tailwind on base. At that low altitude, be reluctant to bank more than 30°, do not skid to fix an overshoot, and treat a go-around as the safest action [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: Application: before every intercept, have the learner say the plan aloud: final course, intercept heading and the cue to start the turn. A missing plan is the overshoot you will see next.

check.q: With the GPS in approach mode, ATC offers your learner a vector to intercept 1 NM outside the FAWP. What do you advise?
check.a: Ask for a wider intercept: being established before the 2 NM sensitivity change avoids confusing CDI indications, and vectors that intercept within 2 NM of the FAWP are not recommended [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17b5(e)(5)]].

chunks.title: Checklists: before, during and after the landing

body.p: **Completion of appropriate checklist items.** A checklist is a memory aid so critical items are not overlooked; it need not be a do-list, since actions can be done and then checked, and before landing and after landing are among the minimum phases that need one [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]. The stabilized approach criteria have every briefing and checklist finished before the approach except the landing checklist [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], and the IPH has crews complete landing checklists early to concentrate on the approach [[29:128|IPH 3-16]].

Items
Source
rows: Before the approach
Weather, NOTAMs, runway length against landing distance, and every briefing and checklist except the landing checklist
Early in the approach
Landing checklist, so attention is free for the approach and the transition

Landing configuration, in trim, stabilized
Final, retractable gear

After-landing checklist only after all parts of the airplane are past the holding position markings

body.p: **Failure to complete required checklist items.** It looks like a landing checklist done late or not at all, a gear or flap item missed, or after-landing items started on the runway. Failure to complete the landing checklist in a timely manner heads the AFH list of approach and landing errors, and many accidents have come from retracting the gear instead of the flaps while still rolling [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. The PTS accepts a review after the items are done when reading the checklist during the maneuver would be unsafe or impracticable for a single pilot, and asks that division of attention and visual scanning be considered when using a checklist (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

callout.text: Application: tie the landing checklist to a fixed point on every approach, such as glideslope intercept or the FAF, and have the learner say "landing checklist complete" aloud. A missing call is your cue, and the learner learns that the checklist belongs before the visual transition, not in it.

check.q: Your learner reads the landing checklist head-down at 300 ft AGL after breaking out. Why is that a problem?
check.a: Everything except the landing checklist should be done before the approach, and the landing checklist should be finished early so the pilot can concentrate on the approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[29:128|IPH 3-16]]. At 300 ft the eyes belong outside with instrument checks, and the PTS wants division of attention considered in checklist use (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).

chunks.title: Positive aircraft control from minimums to a stop

body.p: **Maintenance of positive aircraft control.** Control starts with a stabilized approach. For a typical piston airplane the AFH criteria are a constant glide path, normally 3°; tracking the centerline with bank normally 15° or less; airspeed within +10/-5 knots of the recommended landing speed; landing configuration and in trim; a descent rate generally 500 to 1,000 fpm, reduced before 300 ft AGL if over 500; suitable power; and briefings and checklists done [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Go around if not stabilized by 1,000 ft above airport elevation in IMC; for a typical GA piston airplane in a traffic pattern, the AFH calls for an immediate go-around if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

head: Moment
Positive control means
Source
rows: Low on the path
Add power and raise the nose together; do not retract flaps to fix an undershoot; pitch alone raises the AOA and can cause a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall
High on the path
Reduce power and lower the nose to hold airspeed; add flaps if available
Below 1,000 ft AGL
No descent rate over about 1,000 fpm, in the instrument or the visual part
Round out and touchdown
Eyes not too close (high round out) or too far ahead (low round out); landing attitude before touchdown
Rollout
Rudder or nosewheel steering for direction, aileron toward the wind, firm smooth braking just short of a skid
Go-around
Power, attitude, configuration; forward pressure against the nose-up trim; flaps up in steps

body.p: **Failure to maintain positive aircraft control throughout the complete landing maneuver.** The landing is not over at touchdown: the AFH error list runs through excessive braking and loss of control during touchdown and rollout [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. A rejected landing below the DA or MDA is not necessarily protected by the published missed approach, which assumes a start at or above the MAP and a climb of at least 200 ft per NM [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]], so brief before the approach what the learner will do [[29:180|IPH 4-40]]. A rapid acceleration, such as on takeoff, can create the somatogravic illusion of a nose-up attitude, especially without good visual references, and the disoriented pilot may push into a dive [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]. Application: a go-around back into cloud is the same situation, so the learner must be back on the instruments at once.

callout.text: Positive exchange of flight controls: "You have the flight controls." "I have the flight controls." "You have the flight controls." Brief it before flight, add a visual check, and take the controls calmly when needed [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: In a go-around from a low, slow final, your learner adds full power and the nose rises sharply with left yaw. What is happening, and what is the fix?
check.a: Nose-up approach trim plus full power makes the nose rise sharply and turn left, the elevator trim stall setup [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Hold a safe attitude with considerable forward pressure and right rudder, rough trim, then retract the flaps in steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

body.p: **Demonstrates and simultaneously explains a landing from a straight-in approach from an instructional standpoint.** Your explanation must be clear, concise, technically accurate and complete with no prompting, while you fly to the instrument pilot skill level (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). In the demonstration phase the instructor may describe the actions while doing them, and any deviation from the explanation should be acknowledged and explained at once [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].
**A talk-through you can use** (Application: an example script, not a source procedure; an ILS to Runway 27 with the wind from 300; put in your POH speeds, flaps and checklists):

bullets: "Before the FAF: landing checklist complete, configured, trimmed, on speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. The approach lights are a MALSR, so I expect no red bars [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]]. Wind from the right, so I'm holding a crab."
"On the localizer and glideslope. My scan stays on the instruments; I glance ahead only briefly where the lights should appear [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]."

"Minimums: approach lights in sight, visibility good, in position for a normal descent: continuing [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(1)]]. With no red bars I need the threshold, runway lights or another listed reference to go below 100 ft above the touchdown zone [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]."

"Runway in sight. Now outside is primary: aiming point steady, runway shape constant, airspeed check [[24:176|AFH 9-5]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Crab out, wing-low: rudder lines up the nose, aileron holds the centerline [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]."

"Round out, upwind wheel first, aileron into the wind on the rollout, firm smooth braking [[24:188|AFH 9-17]] [[24:189|AFH 9-18]] [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Past the holding position markings, then the after-landing checklist [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]]."

callout.text: Application: after your demonstration, switch to learner tells, instructor does on the next approach, so the learner organizes the steps before having to fly them [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: During your demonstration you look up at minimums and stop talking for 10 seconds while you line up. What does the examiner see?
check.a: An explanation that is not complete and unprompted, a typical reason for unsatisfactory performance (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). The instructor should describe the actions while demonstrating them, in the order they were explained [[25:175|AIH 9-5]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

body.p: **Analyzes and corrects simulated common errors related to landing from a straight-in approach.** The evaluator acts as your student during selected maneuvers to see how you analyze and correct simulated errors (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Name the error, describe what you see, give the likely cause and the fix, and say how you would teach it.

body.p: Analyze before you correct: when the learner thinks aloud you can tell a misconception from a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Safety permitting, letting a learner go partway into a mistake and find the way out teaches more [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], but near the runway that margin is small: guard the controls, never let the learner exceed your limits, and take the controls calmly with "I have the flight controls" [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

callout.text: Go-arounds are delayed by landing expectancy and by pride; the go-around itself becomes dangerous only when delayed or done improperly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The AFH tells instructors to stress early that any approach may end in a go-around [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]], so offer it as a normal option on every approach, not as a grade.

check.q: The examiner, as your learner, looks up at minimums; the airspeed decays 12 knots and the airplane drifts left. Name the error, the cause and the fix.
check.a: Inappropriate division of attention during the transition (K2a): the scan stopped when the eyes went outside, a fixation and omission fault [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Keep flying by instruments while acquiring the references and keep checking airspeed after the switch [[29:179|IPH 4-39]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL, go around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

scenario.title: Night ILS in rain behind a regional jet
scenario.setup: You are a new CFII and the pilot in command on a night training flight in actual instrument conditions. Your instrument learner has about 30 hours of instrument training. The airplane is a fixed-gear four-seat trainer with a POH approach speed of 70 knots and a maximum demonstrated crosswind of 15 knots. The plan is the ILS to Runway 27 at a towered airport: 5,000 by 100 ft, MALSR, four-light PAPI on the left, DA 200 ft above the TDZE. ATIS: wind 300 at 12 gusting 22, visibility 1 mile in rain, ceiling 400 overcast, braking action advisories are in effect, last report medium. Approach says a regional jet is 6 miles ahead on the same ILS.

questions.q: Before the FAF, what should the learner brief about the runway and the advisories?
questions.a: The runway length against the POH landing distance [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]; the braking report used with the airplane's performance, weight, wind and tires, and a request for current information if none is issued [[33:251|AIM 4-3-9]] [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8]]; the MALSR has no red bars, so the approach lights alone allow descent only to 100 ft above the TDZE [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]] [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]; and on the wet runway a slow touchdown with moderate braking after the nosewheel is down [[24:209|AFH 9-38]].

questions.q: What approach speed and flaps do you coach?
questions.a: The AFH adds one-half the gust factor: the gusts are 10 knots over the steady wind, so about 75 knots, with partial flaps in a gusty crosswind and always within the POH [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Check the crosswind component on the chart against the demonstrated value [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

questions.q: How do you coach the regional jet's wake?
questions.a: Stay at or above the jet's final approach path, note its touchdown point and land beyond it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]], checking that the runway beyond that point still leaves room. Vortices end at touchdown [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]], and a crosswind slows the lateral movement of the upwind vortex [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

questions.q: At the DA you call "approach lights, twelve o'clock." The learner looks up and stares at them; the airspeed drops to 64 knots and the airplane drifts left. What do you say and do?
questions.a: Name it as a division of attention error and get the scan going: airspeed, power and the centerline [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. 64 knots is outside the +10/-5 knot band, and if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL the answer is a go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. In rain and gusts a sudden airspeed loss may also be wind shear, so be ready to go missed at the first indication [[23:316|IFH 10-25]].

questions.q: At 150 ft above the TDZE heavier rain hides the runway lights; only the MALSR is in sight. What now?
questions.a: Provided the flight visibility is still at least the chart value [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2)]], the learner may continue on the approach lights to 100 ft above the TDZE, but no lower unless the threshold, runway lights or another listed reference comes into sight [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]; when the requirements are not met below the DA, the missed approach is immediate [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]. A go-around this low is not necessarily protected by the published missed approach [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]], which is why it is briefed before the approach [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].

Collaborative assessment: the learner's self-assessment first, then your detailed assessment and a discussion comparing the two [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Grade each element, such as the decision at minimums, the transition and the crosswind correction, not just the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

skills.do: Fly an approach to minimums under the view-limiting device, then explain while you fly the decision at minimums, the visual transition, the crosswind correction and the landing to a stop, in the order you briefed it and to instrument pilot standards (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction).
skills.practice: Rehearse the talk-through aloud in a simulator, then in the airplane [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. Have another applicant, holding at least a private certificate with the right category and class ratings, act as safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] and call "look up" at minimums, and practice on a gusty day and at night so the explanation holds up under real workload.

skills.do: As the evaluator flies the K2 errors (poor division of attention at the transition, missed checklist items, a poorly planned turn to final, wrong wind shear, wake or crosswind technique, loss of control on the landing), name each one, describe what you see, give the cause, the fix and how you would teach it.
skills.practice: Take turns with another applicant flying the errors in the table on purpose and correcting them aloud, separating misconceptions from motor-skill errors [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]; debrief each run with collaborative assessment [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Your learner asks what the approach lights are for. Which answer matches the AIM?
options: Proof that obstacles below the MDA are clear
A substitute for the required flight visibility
The basic means to change from instruments to visual
A backup glidepath when the glideslope fails
quiz.why: ALS provide the basic means to transition from instrument flight to visual flight for landing [[33:121|AIM 2-1-1]]. They prove nothing about obstacles, since there is no implicit obstacle protection below the MDA or DA [[33:413|AIM 5-4-5i]], and flight visibility is a separate test [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2)]].

quiz.q: Flying single pilot near minimums, how should your learner use the instruments while looking for the runway?
options: Keep flying by them while acquiring the references
Look outside full time from 200 ft above minimums
Stop the scan at minimums and fly visually from there
Use them only after the runway is in sight
quiz.why: A single pilot must continue to fly by the instruments while attempting to acquire a visual reference [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]. The 100 to 200 ft figure is when a crew's pilot monitoring looks mostly outside, while the pilot flying stays on the instruments [[29:179|IPH 4-39]].

quiz.q: At the DA your learner sees only a MALSR, which has no red bars. How low may they go on those lights alone?
options: To touchdown, if the visibility is legal
To 100 ft above the TDZE
To 200 ft above the airport elevation
To 50 ft above the runway threshold
quiz.why: On the approach lights alone, no descent below 100 ft above the touchdown zone elevation unless the red terminating or side row bars are also visible [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]], and a MALSR shows no red [[23:282|IFH Figure 9-36]]. Below that another listed reference, such as the threshold or runway lights, is needed [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)]].

quiz.q: Tower reports 1 mile and the chart requires 1 mile, but at the MDA your learner judges the flight visibility at about 1/2 mile with runway lights in sight. What is correct?
options: Continue: the reported visibility meets the chart
Continue to 100 ft above the TDZE, then decide
Continue, since a listed reference is distinctly visible
Go missed: flight visibility is below the minimum
quiz.why: Only the pilot can judge whether flight visibility meets the chart; if it is less, go missed regardless of the reported visibility [[23:313|IFH 10-22]]. A reference in sight is only one of the three tests; flight visibility is another [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(2)]].

quiz.q: On the ILS a tailwind shears to a headwind, as in the left picture. What will your learner see?
options: Airspeed up, nose up, a balloon above the glidepath
Airspeed down, sinking below the glidepath
No airspeed change, only a heading correction
Airspeed up while sinking below the glidepath
quiz.why: A shear from a tailwind to a headwind raises the airspeed and pitches the nose up, ballooning the airplane above the glidepath; a headwind shearing to a tailwind does the opposite [[23:316|IFH 10-25]].

quiz.q: Tower says: "Wind shear alert, airport wind 230 at 8, south boundary wind 170 at 20." What should your learner know about the system behind it?
options: It is TDWR, which detects only departure microbursts
It is ASOS, giving the threshold wind only
It is LLWAS, which gives no microburst alerts
It is LLWAS, which covers 20 miles around the field
quiz.why: The airport wind followed by the boundary wind is the LLWAS format, and LLWAS gives wind shear and gust front information but no microburst alerts [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7]] [[33:250|AIM 4-3-7]]. It covers only the periphery of the airport, not 20 miles [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7]].

quiz.q: Your learner will land behind a larger jet that is taking off on the same runway. Where should they plan to touch down?
options: Beyond the point where the jet rotates
Well before the jet's rotation point
Right at the jet's rotation point
Anywhere: the wake begins only at landing
quiz.why: Landing behind a departing larger aircraft on the same runway, note its rotation point and land well prior to it [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Vortices begin at rotation, so beyond that point the wake is waiting [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]].

quiz.q: Tower gives Runway 27 condition codes 5, 3, 3. Using the RCAM, what braking does a code of 3 describe?
options: Good
Good to medium
Poor
Medium
quiz.why: RwyCC 3 matches noticeably reduced braking or directional control, a pilot report of medium [[33:252|AIM FIG 4-3-7]]. The codes are given for the touchdown, mid-point and roll-out zones [[33:251|AIM 4-3-9]]; in the matrix 5 is good and 1 is poor [[33:252|AIM FIG 4-3-7]].

quiz.q: Using the AFH example, the normal approach speed is 70 knots and the wind gusts are 15 knots. What approach speed does the AFH give?
options: 70 knots
85 knots
77 knots
80 knots
quiz.why: Pilots often use the normal approach speed plus one-half the gust factor: 70 knots with 15 knot gusts gives 77 knots, within the AFM/POH [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. 85 knots adds the whole gust.

quiz.q: When should your learner complete the landing checklist on an instrument approach?
options: After breaking out, so nothing is missed
Early, so they can concentrate on the approach
On short final below 300 ft AGL, as a last check
After landing, while still rolling out
quiz.why: Completing landing checklists early lets the crew concentrate on the approach [[29:128|IPH 3-16]], and the stabilized approach criteria have everything else done before the approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. After-landing items wait until clear of the runway [[24:248|AFH 12-17]].

quiz.q: In practice your learner goes quiet at minimums and the airspeed decays. Which technique shows you whether it is a misconception or a motor-skill error?
options: Taking the controls to demonstrate
A written quiz on 91.175 after the flight
Lifting the view-limiting device earlier
Having the learner think aloud while flying
quiz.why: In learner tells, learner does, the thinking is done aloud, which makes it easy to tell whether an error comes from a misconception or a lack of motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

quiz.q: Lining up with an offset runway, your learner overshoots the centerline and adds bottom rudder to tighten the turn. What does the AFH say?
options: Do not skid to fix it; go around
Steepen the bank past 45° instead
Fine, if the ball is kept centered
Slip toward the runway, nose high
quiz.why: Bottom rudder in an overshooting base-to-final turn is the skidding cross-control stall setup; the safest action for an overshoot is a go-around, and at that altitude the pilot should not skid and should be reluctant to bank more than 30° [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: In the AWH wind shear accident shown, what happened at point 3?
options: The crew added thrust and ballooned above the path
The runway lights were taken for a road at night
Airspeed loss and fewer visual cues lowered the pitch
The crew flew the glideslope below minimums too closely
quiz.why: At point 3 the airspeed decrease combined with reduced visual cues resulted in a pitch attitude reduction [[28:271|AWH 22-16]]. The AWH adds that pitch increase and recovery came too late and the transition to outside references may have detracted from the scan [[28:272|AWH 22-17]].

quiz.q: At the break-out your learner sees the runway as in the left picture: long and narrow. What does it mean?
options: Too low: the approach is getting shallow
Too high: the approach is getting steep
Drifting left of the centerline
On the glide path, since the shape is normal
quiz.why: If the approach is steepened the runway appears longer and narrower; if it becomes shallow, shorter and wider [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. The AFH labels the left view too high [[24:177|AFH Figure 9-7]].

final_quiz.q: An approach has only circling minimums, but your learner sees the runway early and is cleared to land straight in. What does the AIM say?
options: They must circle, as no straight-in minimums exist
They may land straight in, with time for a normal approach
They may land straight in only if RVR is reported
They must cancel IFR before landing straight in
final_quiz.why: No published straight-in minimum does not preclude a straight-in landing with the runway in sight and time for a normal approach, once cleared to land on that runway [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks why a VOR approach whose course points straight at the runway shows only circling minimums. Which reason fits the AIM?
options: The VOR is more than 5 NM from the runway
No VDP could be published for the runway
The runway has no approach light system
A normal descent from the IFR altitude isn't possible
final_quiz.why: Straight-in minimums need the course within 30° of the runway and a normal descent to the runway; when the descent rate is exceeded, only circling minimums are published [[33:449|AIM 5-4-20c]]. An aligned procedure may be limited to circling by an excessive descent gradient [[33:414|AIM 5-4-5k4]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot ahead reported a microburst loss on final 2 minutes ago. Your learner says it has probably died out. What do you teach?
options: It keeps strengthening for about 5 minutes
Microbursts last about one minute, so it has passed
One report means another microburst is unlikely
Microburst reports apply only to departures
final_quiz.why: A microburst intensifies for about 5 minutes after it strikes the ground, and once activity starts, more microbursts in the same area should be expected [[34:108|AIM 7-1-24]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner meets wind shear on short final. Which report does the AIM recommend?
options: "Negative wind shear on final"
"Positive wind shear, unstable approach"
"Wind shear, loss of 20 knots at 400"
"Moderate turbulence on final, Cessna"
final_quiz.why: State the loss or gain of airspeed and the altitude; "negative wind shear" has been taken to mean no wind shear at all [[34:106|AIM 7-1-22]].

final_quiz.q: A larger airplane just made a low approach to your runway in a light quartering wind. How long should your learner wait before landing?
options: At least 2 minutes
At least 30 seconds
At least 5 minutes
None, once cleared to land
final_quiz.why: Vortices settle and move along the runway after a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, especially in light quartering wind; ensure at least 2 minutes before landing [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. A landing clearance does not change that: the pilot is ultimately responsible for maintaining an appropriate interval [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks which jet ahead leaves the strongest wake. What do you answer?
options: A light jet, flaps down, flying fast
A heavy jet, flaps up, flying slow
A heavy jet, flaps down, flying fast
A light jet, clean and slow
final_quiz.why: The greatest vortex strength comes from an aircraft that is heavy, clean and slow; a dirty configuration hastens wake decay [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane's main tires are at 49 psi. Using the PHAK formula, about what is the minimum dynamic hydroplaning speed?
options: 44 knots
49 knots
54 knots
63 knots
final_quiz.why: Nine times the square root of the tire pressure: 9 × 7 = 63 knots [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. 54 knots is the PHAK's own example for 36 psi.

final_quiz.q: In the wing-low crosswind method, which control does which job?
options: Aileron aligns the nose; rudder stops the sideways drift
Rudder holds the altitude; aileron holds the airspeed
Rudder aligns the nose; aileron stops the drift
Power stops the drift; rudder sets the descent
final_quiz.why: Rudder aligns and holds the heading with the runway, and aileron sets just enough bank to cancel the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

final_quiz.q: In a strong crosswind, full opposite rudder no longer stops the turn in your learner's sideslip. What does the AFH say?
options: Add flaps to make the rudder more effective
The wind is too strong: use another runway
Crab and hold the crab through touchdown
Steepen the bank until the drift stops
final_quiz.why: If full opposite rudder does not prevent a turn, the wind is too strong for that runway; land on a more favorable runway or at an alternate [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. A crab must be removed just before touchdown, not held through it [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

final_quiz.q: On an approach in IMC, by what height does the AFH say to be stabilized, or else go around?
options: 500 ft above the airport elevation
300 ft above ground level on final
At the published decision altitude
1,000 ft above airport elevation
final_quiz.why: Go around if unable to establish a stabilized approach by 1,000 ft above airport elevation in IMC or 500 ft in VMC; for a typical piston airplane in a traffic pattern, an approach that becomes unstabilized below 300 ft AGL calls for an immediate go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner goes around at 80 ft above the runway when the rain hides it. Does the published missed approach protect them?
options: Yes: it protects any missed approach flown on the course
Yes, if they climb at least 200 ft per NM all the way
Not necessarily: it assumes a start at or above the MAP
No: they must climb straight ahead to the MSA first
final_quiz.why: The published missed approach provides obstacle clearance only when it starts at or above the MAP and climbs at least 200 ft per NM; from below the MDA or DA, clearance is not necessarily provided [[33:451|AIM 5-4-21h]] [[29:180|IPH 4-40]].

final_quiz.q: When does the tower put "braking action advisories are in effect" on the ATIS?
options: After medium, poor or nil reports, or fast-changing braking
Whenever any rain at all is reported on the airport
Only when a FICON NOTAM shows nil braking on a runway
Only at airports that are certificated under 14 CFR Part 139
final_quiz.why: The statement goes on the ATIS when the tower receives reports of medium, poor or nil, or when weather is conducive to deteriorating or rapidly changing braking [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8]]. At federally obligated and Part 139 airports a nil condition on a paved runway is handled by closing the surface, not by a FICON braking NOTAM [[33:250|AIM 4-3-8]].

final_quiz.q: Flying into a fog bank on short final, your learner feels the nose pitching up. What does the IFH warn they may do?
options: Fly a shallower, flatter approach
Steepen the approach abruptly
Misjudge the runway as wider
Level off high and float long
final_quiz.why: Flying into fog can create an illusion of pitching up, and pilots who do not recognize it often steepen the approach quite abruptly [[23:76|IFH 3-9]].

final_quiz.q: Low and slow on short final, your learner reaches to raise the flaps "for less drag." What do you say?
options: Good: less drag will stretch the glide to the runway
Fine, as long as the airspeed stays above 1.3 VSO
No: power and pitch; raising flaps can cause a sink
Raise them halfway first, then add some power
final_quiz.why: When low, increase pitch and power together; retracting the flaps to correct an undershoot may cause a sudden decrease in lift and an excessive sink rate [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: On the checkride, how does the PTS say the evaluator will test your ability to divide attention?
options: By failing a gyro on every approach that is flown
By covering the airspeed indicator on short final
By oral questions on distractions, not in flight
By causing a realistic distraction in flight
final_quiz.why: The evaluator shall cause a realistic distraction during the flight to evaluate division of attention while maintaining safe flight (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). The AIH describes the same FAA policy and the instructor's job of teaching it [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

takeaways: The visual segment is part of the approach: below the DA or MDA it is flown by natural vision under 91.175(c), with no implicit obstacle protection.
Single pilot, keep flying by the instruments while looking for the references. Application: once a required reference is identified, outside is primary and the instruments check it.
Teach the transition in steps: brief the picture, call the references for the learner, then let the learner tell and do.
Brief the environmental, operational and weather factors before the approach: illusions, runway against landing distance, wind, fog and storms.
Treat advisories as decisions: NOTAMs, braking reports and RwyCC, wind shear alerts and wake cautions each change the plan.
Wind shear: go missed at the first sign. Wake: at or above the leader's path, land beyond its touchdown point. Crosswind: wing-low to touchdown.
Landing checklist early, the turn to final planned and led, stabilized or go around, and positive control all the way to the stop.
Demonstrate while explaining in the briefed order; name each error, its cause and its fix.
cfi_notes: The IPH describes the transition for two-pilot crews (pilot flying and pilot monitoring) and says single-pilot operations are harder [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]; no source here gives a single-pilot scan pattern or callouts for it. The sequence and callouts in this lesson are teaching advice built on that crew model.
The PHAK gives the effect of 10% excess landing speed two ways on the same page: "at least a 21 percent increase" and "20 percent" [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Teach about 20%, at least.

The AWH's wind shear encounter analysis describes crewed airplanes: it cites crew coordination and stick shaker activation [[28:272|AWH 22-17]] [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. For a light airplane the sources only say be alert early, be ready to go missed at the first indication, and that recovery at low altitude may be impossible [[23:316|IFH 10-25]] [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. Teach avoidance and an early missed approach, and use the POH for any specific technique.

AIM 7-4-8e (on or above the glidepath, a landing point at least 1,000 ft down the runway, a line of sight above the heavier aircraft) is written for lighter aircraft on visual approaches [[34:153|AIM 7-4-8]]. On an instrument approach, teach 7-4-6: at or above the larger aircraft's path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

The IFH example of a 1/4 mile increase with the ALSF-1 out [[23:313|IFH 10-22]] matches the inoperative components table the IFH reprints, a TPP page dated March 2012 [[23:50|IFH 1-31]]; teach learners to use the table inside the front cover of the current TPP [[23:313|IFH 10-22]], plus the chart notes and NOTAMs. The IFH also still says A/FD [[23:281|IFH 9-38]]; it is now the Chart Supplement [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

How it is tested: Task E is combined with Tasks A and B, and the evaluator may call for a landing or a missed approach after each approach. The view-limiting device does not apply to elements that need visual references, so brief when it comes off (FAA-S-8081-9E, Area VIII NOTE and Introduction). The evaluator acts as your student to test error analysis.

PTS emphasis: the evaluator must emphasize your ability to teach spatial disorientation, wake turbulence and low-level wind shear avoidance, checklist usage and positive exchange of flight controls, and must create a realistic distraction during the flight (FAA-S-8081-9E, Introduction). Expect oral questions on each in this Task.

Examiners like to ask: what you need to see at the DA with a MALSR, flight visibility versus reported visibility, how you would coach a learner who stares at the runway, what an LLWAS alert does and does not cover, how to read a RwyCC report, and how to land behind a departing jet.
gaps: AC 00-54 (Pilot Windshear Guide) and AC 91-79 (runway overruns) are not in the build sources, so no light-airplane wind shear escape procedure and no contaminated-runway landing distance factors are taught; use the POH/AFM.
No source here gives a single-pilot scan pattern or callout set for the instrument-to-visual transition; the steps and callouts in this lesson are labeled teaching advice.
The CFII PTS gives no numeric tolerances for this Task; the stabilized approach numbers come from the AFH for a typical piston airplane.
Approach speeds, flap settings, the maximum demonstrated crosswind, landing distance data and checklists come from the airplane's POH/AFM, which is not in these sources.
No source here says how ATC applies wake turbulence separation behind a larger aircraft on an IFR approach; the lesson teaches only the pilot's avoidance procedures from AIM 7-4.

activities.title: Continue or go around?
activities.intro: Tap each situation at or below minimums, then tap what the learner should do.

items.t: At the DA: approach lights and runway lights in sight, visibility at the chart value, on the glidepath
At 150 ft above TDZE: only a MALSR in sight, visibility at the chart value
Approach becomes unstabilized at 200 ft AGL
At 80 ft above TDZE: only a MALSR in sight, no red bars
Below the MDA: flight visibility drops below the chart value
Short final: a vehicle enters the runway
Below the DA: on speed, on the PAPI glidepath, runway in sight
Near a rain shaft: airspeed jumps 15 knots, then starts to fall

activities.why: Continuing needs all three 91.175(c) tests, and the approach lights alone carry the learner only to 100 ft above TDZE [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i)]]; when the tests are not met below minimums the missed approach is immediate [[60:472|14 CFR 91.175(e)(1)]]. An unstabilized approach or an obstruction on the runway calls for a rejected landing [[29:180|IPH 4-40]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], and at the first sign of wind shear be ready to go missed [[23:316|IFH 10-25]].

activities.title: Read the runway picture
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Too high: runway long and narrow
Too low: runway short and wide
Horizon: scan here from the aiming point

activities.why: A steepening approach makes the runway look longer and narrower and a shallow one shorter and wider [[24:176|AFH 9-5]] [[24:177|AFH Figure 9-7]]. Scan from the aiming point to the horizon and back, and glance at the airspeed periodically [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

activities.title: Runway condition codes
activities.intro: Tap a runway condition code, then tap the braking action it matches.
activities.why: The RCAM matches each code to a pilot-reported braking action [[33:252|AIM FIG 4-3-7]]; codes run from 6 (dry) to 1 (poor), and 0 marks a nil report [[33:251|AIM 4-3-9]].

activities.title: True or false: wind shear and wake
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Every LLWAS installation gives microburst alerts.
cards.why: False. Basic LLWAS gives wind shear and gust front information but no microburst alerts [[33:249|AIM 4-3-7]].

cards.s: A headwind shear followed by a tailwind is especially dangerous after the pilot has reduced power for the headwind.
cards.why: True. It leaves the airplane nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits [[23:316|IFH 10-25]].

cards.s: Microbursts always come with heavy rain you can see.
cards.why: False. They can come from benign-looking cells with little or no rain; a ring of blowing dust may be the only clue [[34:107|AIM 7-1-24]] [[34:108|AIM 7-1-24]].

cards.s: Wake vortices begin at rotation and end at touchdown.
If the tower gives no wake turbulence caution, the pilot need not adjust the flight path.
cards.why: False. Whether or not a warning is given, the pilot is expected to adjust [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

cards.s: A light quartering tailwind can move a preceding aircraft's vortices into the touchdown zone.
cards.why: True, and it requires maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

activities.title: Numbers for the landing
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: POH approach speed 65 knots; the wind is gusting with a gust factor of 10 knots. Using the AFH rule, what approach speed?
items.why: Add one-half the gust factor: 65 + 5 = 70 knots, within the AFM/POH [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

items.q: Main tire pressure 30 psi. About what is the minimum dynamic hydroplaning speed?
VSO is 50 knots. What 90° crosswind must the airplane have shown it can handle in certification testing?
Landing distance at the planning weight is 1,300 ft. You land 10% heavier. About what distance should you expect?
items.why: A 10% increase in landing weight gives about a 10% increase in landing distance: 1,300 × 1.1 = 1,430 ft [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

items.q: On a 3° path, how high above the TDZE should the airplane be 1.5 NM from the threshold?

activities.title: Go around from short final
activities.intro: Put the go-around steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Apply full or maximum allowable power smoothly, without hesitation
Hold a safe climb attitude against the nose-up trim with forward pressure and right rudder, then rough trim
Retract the flaps partially or to the takeoff setting, in steps
With a positive rate of climb and the airplane sure to stay airborne, retract the landing gear
Tell ATC and fly the missed approach or the instructions given
activities.why: Power, attitude, configuration: power first, attitude held against the trim, rough trim, flaps in increments, then gear once the airplane will stay airborne [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Then advise ATC and request further clearance [[23:312|IFH 10-21]].

activities.title: Checkride: the examiner flies the errors
activities.intro: You are the CFII applicant. The examiner, playing your learner, flies an ILS to a landing in a right crosswind and makes errors on purpose. Choose what you say each time.

steps.s: On vectors, the examiner starts the turn late and flies straight through the localizer course.
options: Fine: overshooting a localizer is normal
Name it: a poorly planned turn to final; lead the turn as the needle moves
Have the examiner descend to the glideslope altitude now
Switch to the GPS map and ignore the localizer
steps.why: Pilots learn to lead the turn to prevent overshooting the course [[23:257|IFH 9-14]], and the narrow localizer course, normally 5°, gives high needle sensitivity [[23:280|IFH 9-37]].

steps.s: At glideslope intercept the landing checklist is not done; the examiner says it will be easier once the runway is in sight.
options: Name it: do it now, before the visual transition
Fine: it is quicker once the runway is visible
Skip it: the gear is fixed anyway
Do it at 100 ft above the TDZE
steps.why: Landing checklists are completed early so the pilot can concentrate on the approach [[29:128|IPH 3-16]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; failure to complete the landing checklist in a timely manner is a listed error [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

steps.s: At the DA you lift the device. The examiner stares at the runway; the airspeed decays 10 knots and the airplane drifts left.
options: Fine: below minimums only outside references matter
Put the device back on and continue on instruments
Division of attention: keep the scan, check airspeed, fix the drift
Add flaps to slow down and steepen the approach
steps.why: A single pilot keeps flying by the instruments while acquiring the references [[29:179|IPH 4-39]]; staring at one reference and dropping instruments are cross-check faults [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]], and the stabilized criteria keep airspeed within +10/-5 knots of the landing speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

steps.s: At 300 ft AGL the examiner, crabbed for the right crosswind, kicks the nose straight with the wings level.
options: Fine: aligning the nose early is the goal
Add left aileron to stay in the crab
Go around: crosswinds can't be landed off an ILS
Name it: drifting; lower the right wing and use rudder to align
steps.why: Wing-low: rudder aligns the nose and aileron into the wind stops the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]; inadequate drift correction and touching down while drifting are listed errors [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

steps.s: Just after touchdown on the wet runway the examiner brakes hard and the wheels start to skid.
options: Release brake pressure, let the wheels spin up, steer with rudder
Hold full brakes to stop in the shortest distance
Pump the brakes on and off rapidly
Push forward on the yoke to load the nosewheel
steps.why: Skidding is stopped by releasing the brake pressure; pumping does not improve braking [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. At the first sign of a skid release the brakes, let the wheels spin up and keep directional control with rudder [[24:209|AFH 9-38]]; forward yoke pressure invites wheelbarrowing [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
